arXiv:1705.08415v4 [stat.ML] 24 May 2018

Supervised Community Detection with Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks

Zhengdao Chen Affiliation: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: New York University, New York, NY    Lisha Li Affiliation: Amplify Partners Affiliation: San Francisco, CA    Joan Bruna Affiliation: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: New York University, New York, NY
Abstract

We study data-driven methods for supervised community detection on graphs. This estimation problem is typically formulated in terms of the spectrum of certain operators, as well as with posterior inference under certain probabilistic graphical models. Focusing on random graph families such as the Stochastic Block Model, recent research has unified both approaches, and identified both statistical and computational signal-to-noise detection thresholds.

We identify the resulting class of algorithms with a family of Graph Neural Networks and show that they can reach those detection thresholds in a purely data-driven manner, without access to the underlying generative models and with no parameter assumptions. For that purpose, we propose to augment GNNs with the non-Backtracking operator, defined on the line graph of edge adjacencies. We also perform the first analysis of optimization landscape on a simplified GNN family, revealing an interesting transition from rugged to simple as the graph size increases. Finally, the resulting model is also tested on real datasets, performing significantly better than rigid parametric models.

   

1 Introduction

Graph inference problems encompass a large class of tasks and domains, from posterior inference in probabilistic graphical models to community detection and ranking in generic networks, image segmentation, or graph inverse problems. They are motivated both by practical applications, such as PageRank, but also by fundamental complexity questions, which ask for the intrinsic algorithmic hardness of solving a certain class of graph inference tasks.

These problems can be formulated in either unsupervised, semi-supervised or purely supervised learning settings. In the latter, one assumes a dataset of graphs with labels on its nodes and/or edges, and attempts to perform node/edge classification by optimizing a loss over a certain parametric class, e.g. neural networks. Graph Neural Networks ([10], [3] and references therein) are natural extensions of Convolutional Neural Networks to graph-structured data, and have emerged as a powerful class of algorithms to perform complex graph inference leveraging labeled data. In essence, these neural networks learn cascaded linear combinations of intrinsic graph operators interleaved with node-wise (or edge-wise) activation functions. Since they learn from intrinsic graph operators, they can be applied to varying input graphs, and they offer the same parameter sharing advantages as their CNN counterparts.

In this work, we focus on community detection problems, a wide class of node classification tasks that attempt to discover a clustered, segmented structure within a network or graph. The algorithmic approaches to this problem include a rich class of spectral methods – which relate the solution to the spectrum of certain operators defined on the graph; as well as approximate message-passing methods such as Belief-Propagation, which perform approximate posterior inference under predefined graphical models. Focusing on the supervised setting, we study the ability of GNNs to approximate, generalize (or even improve) upon these class of algorithms. Our motivation is two-fold: on the one hand, this problem exhibits algorithmic hardness on some settings, opening up the possibility to discover more efficient algorithms than are currently known in some regimes. On the other hand, many practical scenarios fall beyond pre-specified probabilistic models, requiring data-driven solutions.

First, we propose key modifications to the GNN architecture allowing it to exploit edge adjacency information through the so-called non-backtracking operator of the graph. This operator is defined over the edges of the graph and allows a directed flow of information, even when the original graph is undirected. We refer to this extension as hierarchical GNN since it amounts to defining a GNN on the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of GG, a particular graph hierarchy used in Complexity theory. Focusing on important random graph families exhibiting community structure, such as the Stochastic Block Model and the Geometric Block Model, we demonstrate improvements in the resulting accuracy, even in regimes within the so-called computational-to-statistical gap. A perhaps surprising aspect is that these gains can be obtained even with linear GNNs, which become parametric versions of power iteration algorithms.

This motivates our second main contribution: the analysis of the optimization landscape of such linear GNN models when trained with planted solutions of a given graph distribution. We show that these landscapes have an interesting property, namely the presence of an energy gap controlling the energy between local and global minima. This energy gap shrinks with the concentration of certain graph spectral properties, supporting the fact that the optimization landscape is benign on large enough graphs.

Summary of Main Contributions:

  • •

    We propose an extension of GNNs that operate on the line graph using the non-backtracking operator, which yields significant improvements on hard community detection regimes.

  • •

    We show that on the Stochastic Block-Model we reach detection thresholds in a purely data-driven fashion, we significantly improve upon Belief-Propogation on hard SBM detection regimes, as well as in the Geometric Block Model.

  • •

    We perform the first analysis of the learning landscape of GNN models, showing that they exhibit a form of ‘energy gap’, where local mimima are confined in low-energy configurations.

  • •

    We show how our model can be applied to real-world datasets, leading to state-of-the-art community detection results.

2 Problem Setup

We are interested in a specific class of node-classification tasks in which given an input graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), a signal y:V→{1,C}y:V\to\{1,C\} encoding a partition of VV into CC groups is to be predicted at each node. We assume that a training set {(Gt,yt)}t≤T\{(G_{t},y_{t})\}_{t\leq T} is given, which we use to learn a model y^=Φ⁡(G,θ)\hat{y}=\Phi(G,\theta) trained by minimising

L⁡(θ)=1T​∑t≤Tℓ⁡(Φ⁡(Gt,θ),yt).L(\theta)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t\leq T}\ell(\Phi(G_{t},\theta),y_{t})~.

Since yy encodes a partition of CC groups, the specific label of each node is only important up to a global permutation of {1,C}\{1,C\}. Section 4.3 describes how to construct losses ℓ⁡(a,b)\ell(a,b) with such a property. A permutation of the observed nodes translates into the same permutation applied to the labels, which justifies models Φ\Phi that are equivariant to permutations. Also, we are interested in inferring properties of community detection algorithms that do not depend on the specific size of the graphs11 1 In this work, however, we assume that CC is fixed.. We therefore require that the model Φ\Phi accepts graphs of variable size for the same set of parameters, similarly as in sequential RNN or spatial CNN models. In our study of random graph models (SBM and GBM), we construct a training set of planted solutions. Labels yiy_{i} are generated by sampling a balanced partition uniformly at random, and then we produce the input graphs GiG_{i} by sampling Gi|yiG_{i}|y_{i} according to each random graph model.

3 Related Work

The GNN was first proposed in [10, 28]. [4] generalized convolutional neural networks on general undirected graphs by using the graph Laplacian’s eigenbasis. This was the first time the Laplacian operator was used in a neural network architecture to do classification on graph input. [7] considers a symmetric Laplacian generator to define a multiscale GNN architecture, demonstrated on classification tasks. Similarly, [15] uses a similar generator as effective embedding mechanisms for graph signals, applied on semi-supervised tasks. This is the closest application of GNNs to our current contribution. However, we highlight that semi-supervised learning requires bootstrapping the estimation with a subset of labeled nodes, and is mainly interested in generalization within a single, fixed graph. On the other hand, our setup treats community detectection across a distribution of input graphs and assumes no initial labeling on a given test-set input graph. There have been several extensions of GNNs [18, 31, 8, 24] by modifying their non-linear activation functions, their parameter sharing strategies, and their choice of graph operators. In particular, [9] interpreted the GNN architecture as learning an approximate message-passing algorithm, which in particular extend the learning of hidden representations to graph edges besides graph nodes. Another recent related work is [16], which proposes a generalization of GNN that captures high-order node interactions through covariant tensor algebra. Our approach to extend the expressive power of GNN using the line graph may be seen as an alternative.

Our Energy landscape analysis is related to the recent [29], which establishes an energy bound on the local minima arising in resnets. In our case, we exploit the specific properties of the problem to produce an energy bound that provably shrinks with the size of the input graphs. Finally, [38] works on data regularization for clustering and rank estimation and is also motivated by success of using Bethe-Hessian-like perturbations to improve spectral methods on sparse networks. They find good perturbations via matrix perturbations, and also had success on the Stochastic Blockmodel. Leskovec and coauthors have done a lot of work in community detection in curating benchmark datasets, quantifying the quality of these datasets[35], and also in making new algorithms for community detection by fitting data to newly designed generative models (models that exhibit similar statistical structure learned from their analysis of the aforementioned datasets)[34].

4 Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks

This section introduces our GNN architectures based on the power graph adjacency (Section 4.1) and its extension to line graphs using the non-Backtracking operator (Section 4.2), as well as the design of losses invariant to global label permutations (Section 4.3).

4.1 Power Graph Neural Networks

The Graph Neural Network (GNN), introduced in [28] and later simplified in [19, 8, 32] is a flexible neural network architecture that is based on local operators on a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E). We start by briefly reviewing the generic GNN architecture, and next describe our modifications to make it suitable to our interests. Given some input signal x∈ℝ|V|×bx\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times b} on the vertices of GG, we consider graph intrinsic linear operators that act locally on this signal: The degree operator is the linear map D:F↦D​FD:F\mapsto DF where (D​x)i:=d​e​g​(i)⋅xi,D⁡(x)=diag​(A​𝟏)​x.(Dx)_{i}:=deg(i)\cdot x_{i}~,~D(x)=\text{diag}(A{\bf 1})x~. The adjacency operator AA is the linear map given by the adjacency matrix Ai,j=1A_{i,j}=1 iff (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E. Similarly, JJ-th powers of AA encode JJ-hop neighborhoods of each node, and allow us to combine and aggregate local information at different scales. We consider in this work the power graph adjacency Aj=min⁡(1,A2j)A_{j}=\min(1,A^{2^{j}}), which encodes 2j2^{j}-hop neighborhoods into a binary graph.

We consider a multiscale GNN layer that receives as input a signal x(k)∈ℝ|V|×bkx^{(k)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|V|\times b_{k}} and produces x(k+1)∈ℝ|V|×bk+1x^{(k+1)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|V|\times b_{k+1}} as

x(k+1)i,l\displaystyle{x^{(k+1)}}_{i,l} =\displaystyle= ρ⁡[xi(k)​θ1,l(k)+(D​x(k))i​θ2,l(k)+∑j=0J−1(A2j​x(k))i​θ3+j,l(k)],l=1,…​bk+1/2,i∈V,\displaystyle\rho\left[x^{(k)}_{i}\theta_{1,l}^{(k)}+(Dx^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{2,l}^{(k)}+\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}(A^{2^{j}}x^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{3+j,l}^{(k)}\right],\,l=1,\dots b_{k+1}/2,i\in V, (1)
x(k+1)i,l\displaystyle{x^{(k+1)}}_{i,l} =\displaystyle= xi(k)​θ1,l(k)+(D​x(k))i​θ2,l(k)+∑j=0J−1(A2j​x(k))i​θ3+j,l(k),l=bk+1/2+1,…​bk+1,i∈V,\displaystyle x_{i}^{(k)}\theta_{1,l}^{(k)}+(Dx^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{2,l}^{(k)}+\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}(A^{2^{j}}x^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{3+j,l}^{(k)},\,l=b_{k+1}/2+1,\dots b_{k+1},i\in V,

where Θ={θ1(k),…,θJ+3(k)}\Theta=\{\theta_{1}^{(k)},\dots,\theta_{J+3}^{(k)}\}, θs(k)∈ℝbk×bk+1\theta_{s}^{(k)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{b_{k}\times b_{k+1}} are trainable parameters and ρ⁡(⋅)\rho(\cdot) is a point-wise nonlinearity, chosen in this work to be ρ⁡(z)=max⁡(0,z)\rho(z)=\max(0,z). We thus consider a layer with linear “residual connections" [12], to both ease with the optimization when using large number of layers, but also to give the model the ability to perform power iterations. Since the spectral radius of the learnt linear operators in (1) can grow as the optimization progresses, the cascade of gnn layers can become unstable to training. In order to mitigate this effect, we consider spatial batch normalization [13] at each layer.

As explained in Section A.1, the Krylov subspace generated by the graph Laplacian [7] is not sufficient in this case to operate well in the sparse regime, as opposed to the generators {I,D,A}\{I,D,A\}. The expressive power of each layer is increased by adding multiscale versions of AA, although this benefit comes at the cost of computational efficiency, especially in the sparse regime. The network depth is chosen to be of the order of the graph diameter, so that all nodes obtain information from the entire graph. In sparse graphs with small diameter, this architecture offers excellent scalability and computational complexity. Indeed, in many social networks diameters are constant (due to hubs), or ∼log⁡(|V|)\sim~\log(|V|), as in the Stochastic Block-Model in the constant average degree regime [25]. This results in a model with computational complexity of the order of ∼|V|log(|V)\sim|V|\log(|V), making it amenable to large-scale graphs. In our setup, batch normalization not only prevents gradient blowup, but also performs the orthogonalisation relative to the constant vector, which is associated with the smallest eigenvector of the graph operator whose spectrum contains community information. This reinforces the analogy between cascading layers of (1) and the power iterations to obtain the Fiedler vector of such operator. Indeed, if one wants to extract the Fiedler vector of a matrix MM, whose smallest eigenvector is known to be vv, one can do so by performing power iterations on M~=‖M‖​I−M\tilde{M}=\|M\|I-M as y(n+1)=M~​x(n),x(n+1)=y(n+1)−vT​v​y(n+1)‖y(n+1)−vT​v​y(n+1)‖.y^{(n+1)}=\tilde{M}x^{(n)}~,~x^{(n+1)}=\frac{y^{(n+1)}-v^{T}vy^{(n+1)}}{\|y^{(n+1)}-v^{T}vy^{(n+1)}\|}~. If vv is a constant vector, then the normalization above is precisely performed within the Batch Normalization step.

4.2 GNN on Line Graphs with Non-backtracking Operator

For graphs that have few cycles, posterior inference can be remarkably approximated by loopy Belief Propagation [36]. As described in Section A.2, the message-passing rules are defined over the edge adjacency graph; see equation 7. Although its second-order approximation around the critical point can be efficiently approximated with a power method over the original graph, a data-driven version of BP requires accounting for the non-backtracking structure of the message-passing. In this section we describe how to upgrade the GNN model so that it can exploit non-backtracking operators.

The line graph L⁡(G)=(Vl,El)L(G)=(V_{l},E_{l}) is the graph representing by the edge adjacency structure of GG. If G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is an undirected graph, then the vertices VlV_{l} of L⁡(G)L(G) are the ordered edges in EE, that is Vl={(i→j);(i,j)∈E}∪{(j→i);(i,j)∈E}V_{l}=\{(i\to j);\,(i,j)\in E\}\cup\{(j\to i);\,(i,j)\in E\}, so |Vl|=2​|E||V_{l}|=2|E|. The non-backtracking operator B∈ℝ2​|E|×2​|E|B\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2|E|\times 2|E|} encodes the edge adjacency structure as follows. Two nodes in L⁡(G)L(G) are connected if

B(i→j),(i′→j′)={1if ​j=i′​ and ​j′≠i,0otherwise.B_{(i\to j),(i^{\prime}\to j^{\prime})}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}1&\text{if }j=i^{\prime}\text{ and }j^{\prime}\neq i\,,\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.

This operator thus allows to propagate directed information through the graph. The message-passing rules of BP can be expressed as a diffusion in the line graph L⁡(G)L(G) using this non-backtracking operator, with specific choices of activation function that turn product of beliefs into sums. A natural extension of the GNN architecture presented in Section 4.1 is thus to consider a second GNN defined on L⁡(G)L(G), generated by the corresponding non-backtracking operator BB and degree DB=diag⁡(B​𝟏)D_{B}=\mathrm{diag}(B\mathbf{1}) operators. This effectively defines edge features that are diffused and updated according to the edge adjacency of GG. Edge and node features are combined at each layer using the edge indicator matrices Pm,Pd∈{0,1}|V|×2​|E|\mathrm{Pm},\mathrm{Pd}\in\{0,1\}^{|V|\times 2|E|}, defined as Pmi,(i→j)=1\mathrm{Pm}_{i,(i\to j)}=1, Pmj,(i→j)=1\mathrm{Pm}_{j,(i\to j)}=1, Pdi,(i→j)=1\mathrm{Pd}_{i,(i\to j)}=1, Pdj,(i→j)=−1\mathrm{Pd}_{j,(i\to j)}=-1 and 00 otherwise. Dropping the skip linear connections for ease of exposition, the resulting model becomes

x(k+1)i,l\displaystyle{x^{(k+1)}}_{i,l} =\displaystyle= ρ⁡[xi(k)​θ1,l(k)+(D​x(k))i​θ2,l(k)+∑j=0J−1(A2j​x(k))i​θ3+j,l(k)+{Pm,Pd}​y(k)​θ3+J,l(k)],i∈V\displaystyle\rho\left[x^{(k)}_{i}\theta_{1,l}^{(k)}+(Dx^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{2,l}^{(k)}+\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}(A^{2^{j}}x^{(k)})_{i}\theta_{3+j,l}^{(k)}+\{\mathrm{Pm,Pd}\}y^{(k)}\theta_{3+J,l}^{(k)}\right],\,i\in V (2)
y(k+1)i′,l′\displaystyle{y^{(k+1)}}_{i^{\prime},l^{\prime}} =\displaystyle= ρ⁡[yi′(k)​γ1,l′(k)+(DL⁡(G)​y(k))i′​γ2,l′(k)+∑j=0J−1(AL⁡(G)2j​y(k))i′​γ3+j,l′(k)+[{Pm,Pd}⊤​x(k+1)]i′​γ3+J,l′(k)],i′∈Vl.\displaystyle\rho\left[y_{i^{\prime}}^{(k)}\gamma_{1,l^{\prime}}^{(k)}+(D_{L(G)}y^{(k)})_{i^{\prime}}\gamma_{2,l^{\prime}}^{(k)}+\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}(A_{L(G)}^{2^{j}}y^{(k)})_{i^{\prime}}\gamma_{3+j,l^{\prime}}^{(k)}+[\{\mathrm{Pm,Pd}\}^{\top}x^{(k+1)}]_{i^{\prime}}\gamma_{3+J,l^{\prime}}^{(k)}\right],\,i^{\prime}\in V_{l}.

with additional parameters {γ1(k),…,γJ+3(k)}\{\gamma_{1}^{(k)},\dots,\gamma_{J+3}^{(k)}\}, γs(k)∈ℝbk×bk+1\gamma_{s}^{(k)}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{b_{k}\times b_{k+1}}. It is easy to verify that the resulting model Φ⁡(G):=x(K)\Phi(G):=x^{(K)} satisfies the permutation equivariance property required for the task: Φ⁡(Gπ)=Π​Φ​(G)\Phi(G_{\pi})=\Pi\Phi(G), where Π\Pi is the permutation matrix associated with π\pi. Several authors have proposed combining node and edge feature learning [10, 9, 33], although we are not aware of works that considered the edge adjacency structure provided by the line graph and the non-backtracking operator. For graph families with constant average degree d¯\overline{d}, the line graph has size 2​|E|=d¯​|V|2|E|=\overline{d}|V| of the same order, making this model feasible from the computational point of view. The line graph construction can be iterated with L⁡(L⁡(G)),L⁡(…​L​(G)​…)L(L(G)),L(\dots L(G)\dots) to yield a graph hierarchy, that captures high-order interactions between the elements of GG. Such hierarchical construction relates to other recent efforts to generalize GNNs [16]. Finally, we bootstrap the network by considering the input signal x(0)=deg​(G)x^{(0)}=\text{deg}(G) (and y(0)=deg​(L​(G))y^{(0)}=\text{deg}(L(G)) in the line graph version).

4.3 Label permutation invariant loss

Let 𝒞={c1,…,cC}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{C}\} denote the possible community labelings that each node can take. Consider first the case where communities do not overlap: CC equals the number existing communities. We define the network output at each node using standard softmax, computing the conditional probability that node ii belongs to community cc: oi,c=p⁡(yi=c|θ,G)o_{i,c}=p(y_{i}=c~|\theta,G).Let y∈𝒞Vy\in\mathcal{C}^{V} be the ground truth community structure. Since community belonging is defined up to global label changes in communities, we define the loss associated with a given graph instance as

ℓ(θ)=infπ∈S𝒞−∑i∈Vlogoi,π⁡(yi),\ell(\theta)=\inf_{\pi\in S_{\mathcal{C}}}-\sum_{i\in V}\log o_{i,\pi(y_{i})}~, (3)

where S𝒞S_{\mathcal{C}} denotes the permutation group of CC elements. In our experiments we considered examples with small number of communities C∈{2,5}C\in\{2,5\}, but general scenarios, where CC is suspected to be much larger, might make the evaluation of (3) over the permutation group of CC elements impractical. A possible solution is to randomly partition for each sample C/C~C/\tilde{C} labels into C~\tilde{C} groups, then marginalize the model outputs oi,co_{i,c}, c≤Cc\leq C into o¯i,c¯=∑c∈c¯oi,c\bar{o}_{i,\bar{c}}=\sum_{c\in\bar{c}}o_{i,c} and use ℓ(θ)=infπ∈S𝒞~−∑i∈Vlogo¯i,π⁡(yi¯)\ell(\theta)=\inf_{\pi\in S_{\tilde{\mathcal{C}}}}-\sum_{i\in V}\log\bar{o}_{i,\pi(\bar{y_{i}})} , which only involves a permutation group of size C~!\tilde{C}!. Finally, if we are in a setup where nodes can belong to multiple communities, we simply redefine 𝒞\mathcal{C} to include subsets of communities instead of just singletons, and modify the permutation group S𝒞S_{\mathcal{C}} accordingly.

5 Energy Landscape of Multilinear GNN optimization

As described in the numerical experiments, we found that the GNN models without non-linear activations already provide substantial gains relative to baseline (non-trained) algorithms, by finding suitable generalizations of power iterations. This section studies the optimization landscape resulting from this linear assumption. Despite defining a non-convex objective, we prove that the landscape is ‘benign’ under certain further simplifications, in the sense that the local minima are confined on sublevel sets of low energy.

For simplicity, we consider only the binary c=2c=2 case where we replace the node-wise binary cross-entropy by the squared cosine distance22 2 to account for the invariance up to global flip of label, and we assume a single feature map (dk=1d_{k}=1 for all kk), and focus on the power GNN described in Section 4.1 (although our analysis carries equally to describe the line graph version; see remarks below). We also make the simplifying assumption to replace the layer-wise spatial batch normalization by a simpler projection onto the unit ℓ2\ell_{2} ball (thus we do not remove the mean). Without loss of generality, assume that the input graph GG has size nn, and denote by ℱ={A1,…,AQ}\mathcal{F}=\{A_{1},\dots,A_{Q}\} the family of graph operators appearing in (1). Each layer thus applies an arbitrary polynomial ∑q=1Qθq(k)​Aq\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\theta_{q}^{(k)}A_{q} to the incoming node feature vector x(k)x^{(k)}. Given an input node vector w∈ℝnw\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, the network output can thus be written as

Y^=e‖e‖, with ​e=(∏k=1K∑q≤Qθq(k)​Aq)​w.\hat{Y}=\frac{e}{\|e\|}\,,\text{ with }e=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{q\leq Q}\theta_{q}^{(k)}A_{q}\right)w\,. (4)

In general, the operators in ℱ\mathcal{F} are not commutative, but by considering the generalised Krylov subspace generated by powers of ℱ\mathcal{F}, ℱK={O1=A1K,O2=A1​A2K−1,O3=A1​A2​A1K−2,…​OQK=AQK}\mathcal{F}^{K}=\{O_{1}=A_{1}^{K},O_{2}=A_{1}A_{2}^{K-1},O_{3}=A_{1}A_{2}A_{1}^{K-2},\dots O_{Q^{K}}=A_{Q}^{K}\}, one can reparametrise (4) as e=∑j=1QKβj​Oj​we=\sum_{j=1}^{Q^{K}}\beta_{j}O_{j}w with β∈ℝM\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{M}, with M=QKM=Q^{K}. Given the target y∈ℝny\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, the loss incurred by each pair (G,y)(G,y) becomes |⟨e,y⟩|2‖e‖2\frac{|\langle e,y\rangle|^{2}}{\|e\|^{2}}, and therefore the population loss, when expressed in terms of β\beta, equals

Ln​(β)=𝔼Xn,Yn​β⊤​Yn​ββ⊤​Xn​β,with L_{n}(\beta)=\mathbb{E}_{X_{n},Y_{n}}\frac{\beta^{\top}Y_{n}\beta}{\beta^{\top}X_{n}\beta}~,\text{with } (5)
Yn=zn​zn⊤∈ℝM×M,(zn)j=⟨Oj​w,y⟩​ and ​Xn=Un​Un⊤∈ℝM×M,Un=[(O1​w)⊤…(OM​w)⊤].Y_{n}=z_{n}z_{n}^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{M\times M}\,,\,(z_{n})_{j}=\langle O_{j}w,y\rangle\,\text{ and }X_{n}=U_{n}U_{n}^{\top}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{M\times M}\,,U_{n}=\begin{bmatrix}(O_{1}w)^{\top}\\ \dots\\ (O_{M}w)^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\,.

The landscape is thus specified by a pair of random matrices Yn,Xn∈ℝM×MY_{n},X_{n}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{M\times M}. The following theorem establishes that under appropriate assumptions, the concentration of XnX_{n}, YnY_{n} around their mean controls the energy gaps between local and global maxima of LL.

We define a ‘mean-field’ loss function L~n​(β)=𝔼Xn,Yn​βT​Yn​ββT​𝔼​Xn​β=βT​𝔼​Yn​ββT​𝔼​Xn​β\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta)=\mathbb{E}_{X_{n},Y_{n}}\frac{\beta^{T}Y_{n}\beta}{\beta^{T}\mathbb{E}X_{n}\beta}=\frac{\beta^{T}\mathbb{E}Y_{n}\beta}{\beta^{T}\mathbb{E}X_{n}\beta}, and consider LnL_{n} as a perturbation of L~n\tilde{L}_{n}. Assuming that 𝔼​Xn≻0,∀n\mathbb{E}X_{n}\succ 0,\forall n, we write the Cholesky decomposition of 𝔼​Xn\mathbb{E}X_{n} as 𝔼​Xn=Tn​TnT\mathbb{E}X_{n}=T_{n}T_{n}^{T}, and define An=Tn−1​Yn​(Tn−1)TA_{n}=T_{n}^{-1}Y_{n}(T_{n}^{-1})^{T}, A¯n=𝔼​An=Tn−1​𝔼​Yn​(Tn−1)T\bar{A}_{n}=\mathbb{E}A_{n}=T_{n}^{-1}\mathbb{E}Y_{n}(T_{n}^{-1})^{T}, Bn=Tn−1​Xn​(Tn−1)TB_{n}=T_{n}^{-1}X_{n}(T_{n}^{-1})^{T}, and Δ​Bn=Bn−I\Delta B_{n}=B_{n}-I. Given a symmetric matrix K∈ℝM×MK\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}, ∀i∈{1,…,M}\forall i\in\{1,...,M\}, we let λ1​(K),λ2​(K),…,λM​(K)\lambda_{1}(K),\lambda_{2}(K),...,\lambda_{M}(K) denote the eigenvalues of KK in nondecreasing order.

Theorem 5.1.

Assume that (i) limn→∞[λ1​(A¯n)−λ2​(A¯n)]>0\lim_{n\to\infty}[\lambda_{1}(\bar{A}_{n})-\lambda_{2}(\bar{A}_{n})]>0, (ii) {𝔼⁡[|λ1​(An)|6]}n∈ℕ∗\{\mathbb{E}[|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{6}]\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}} is bounded uniformly, (iii) limn→∞𝔼⁡[‖Δ​Bn‖6]=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{6}]=0 and (iv) {𝔼⁡[1|λM​(Bn)|6]}n∈ℕ∗\{\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{6}}]\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}} is bounded uniformly. Then ∀ϵ>0,∃n∗∈ℕ\forall\epsilon>0,\exists n^{*}\in\mathbb{N} such that ∀n>n∗,∀βl∈𝕊M−1\forall n>n^{*},\forall\beta_{l}\in\mathbb{S}^{M-1}, if βl\beta_{l} is a local maximum of LnL_{n}, and βg\beta_{g} is a global maximum of LnL_{n}, then |Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤ϵ​Ln​(βg)|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq\epsilon L_{n}(\beta_{g}).

The main strategy of the proof is to consider the actual loss function LnL_{n} as a perturbation of L~n\tilde{L}_{n}, which has a landscape that is easier to analyze and does not have poor local maxima, since it is equivalent to a quadratic form defined over the sphere 𝕊M−1\mathbb{S}^{M-1}. For a given graph inverse problem, this theorem thus requires estimating spectral fluctuations of the pair XnX_{n}, YnY_{n}, which in turn involve the spectrum of C∗C^{*} algebras generated by the non-commutative family ℱ\mathcal{F}. That said, one should expect concentration to happen in general, since the dimension MM is fixed as nn grows. Another interesting question is to understand how the asymptotics of our landscape analysis relate to the hardness of estimation as a function of the Signal-to-Noise ratio. Finally, another open question is to what extent our result could be extended to the non-linear residual GNN case, perhaps leveraging ideas from [29].

6 Experiments

We present experiments on synthetic community detection (Sections 6.1, 6.2, 6.3) as well as real-world detection (Section 6.4). In the synthetic experiments, our performance measure is the overlap between predicted (y^\hat{y}) and true labels (yy), which quantifies how much better than random guessing a predicted labelling is. The overlap is given by (1n​∑uδy​(u),y^​(u)−1C)/(1−1C)\big(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{u}\delta_{y(u),\hat{y}(u)}-\frac{1}{C}\big)/(1-\frac{1}{C}) where δ\delta is the Kronecker delta function, and the labels are defined up to global permutation. The GNNs were all trained with 3030 layers, 22 feature maps and J=3J=3 in the middle layers. We used Adamax [14] with learning rate 0.0040.004 across all experiments. 33 3 Code will be publicly released at ???.???.???

6.1 Binary Stochastic Block Model

The Stochastic Block Model is a random graph model with planted community structure. In its simplest form, one assigns |V|=n|V|=n nodes to CC classes at random with Y:V→{1,…,C}Y:V\rightarrow\{1,...,C\} and draws an edge connecting any two vertices u,vu,v independently at random with probability pp if Y⁡(v)=Y⁡(u)Y(v)=Y(u), and with probability qq otherwise. The sparse binary case C=2C=2 when p,q≃1/np,q\simeq 1/n is well understood and provides an initial platform to compare the GNN against provably optimal recovery algorithms; see the supplementary for more information. We consider two learning scenarios. In the first scenario, we train parameters θ\theta conditional on pp and qq, by producing 60006000 samples G∼S​B​M​(n=1000,pi,pi,C=2)G\sim SBM(n=1000,p_{i},p_{i},C=2) for different pairs (pi,qi)(p_{i},q_{i}) and estimating the resulting θ⁡(pi,qi)\theta(p_{i},q_{i}). In the second scenario, reported in the supplementary material, we train a single set of parameters θ\theta from a sample of 60006000 samples containing a mixture of SBM with different parameters p,qp,q and average degree. This setup is important as it shows our GNN is not just approximating known algorithms such as BP, since the parameters are not constant in this dataset. Figure 1 reports the performance of our models on the binary SBM model for different SNR regimes and compares it with the Belief-Progation baseline from [6], as well as the reference normalized laplacian spectral method. We observe that our models reach the statistical detection threshold, given in this case by the BP algorithm. Notice that even the linear GNN matches the performance, in accordance to the spectral approximations of BP given by the Bethe Hessian (see supplementary), and significantly outperforms doing 3030 power iterations on that operator. We notice the line-graph version slightly outperforms the baseline GNN, and that even the linear model that only considers residual connections reaches the statistical threshold. We ran experiments in the disassociative case (q>pq>p), as well as with C=3C=3 communities, and obtained similar results, not reported here.

6.2 Computational-to-Statistical Thresholds in the SBM

The previous section showed that for small number of communities (k<4k<4), the GNN-based model is able to reach the information theoretic (IT) threshold. In such regimes, it is known [1, 20, 5] that BP provably reaches such IT threshold. The situation is different for k>4k>4, where it is conjectured that a computational-to-statistical gap exists between the theoretical performance of MLE estimators and any polynomial-time estimation procedure [6]. In this context, one can use the GNN model to search the space of BP generalizations, and attempt to improve the detection performance of BP for signal-to-noise ratios falling within the computational-to-statistical gap. Table 2 presents results for the 55-community disassociative case, with p=0p=0 and q=18/nq=18/n, and n=400n=400 This amounts to solving a graph coloring problem in a sparse regime, which falls above the IT threshold but below the regime where BP is able to detect [6], asymptotically as n→∞n\to\infty. We see that the GNN models significantly outperform BP in this regime, and that the line GNN version provides the best overlap performance, opening up the possibility to reduce the computation-information gap. That said, our model may be picking finite-size effects, which may vanish as n→∞n\to\infty; the asymptotic study of these gains is left for future work.

6.3 Geometric Block Model

The success of Belief-Propagation on the SBM relies on its locally hyperbolic properties, which make it tree-like with high probability. This behavior is completely different if one considers random graphs with locally Euclidean geometry. The Geometric Block Model [27] is a random graph generated as follows. One starts by sampling nn iid points x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} from a Gaussian mixture model given by means μ1,…​μk∈ℝd\mu_{1},\dots\mu_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at distance SS apart and identity covariances. The labels correspond to which Gaussian each sample belongs to. We draw an edge between two nodes i,ji,j if ‖xi−xj‖≤T/n\|x_{i}-x_{j}\|\leq T/\sqrt{n}. Due to the triangle inequality, the model contains a large number of short cycles, impacting the performance of loopy belief propagation. This motivates other estimation algorithms based on motif-counting [27] that require knowledge of the model likelihood function. Table 2 shows the performance of the GNN models on the binary GBM model, obtained with d=2d=2, n=500n=500, T=5​2T=5\sqrt{2} and varying SS, and its comparison with several spectral methods, including the Bethe Hessian, which approximates BP around its stationary solution. We verify that the line GNN model, thanks to its added flexibility and the multiscale nature of its generators, is able to significantly outperform both spectral methods as well as the baseline GNN.

6.4 Real Datasets from SNAP

We train the GNN on real datasets with community labels provided by SNAP. These datasets have ground truth community labels ranging from social networks to hierarchical co-purchasing networks. We obtain the training set as follows. For each SNAP dataset, we start by focusing only on the 5000 top quality communities provided by the dataset. We then identify edges (i,j)(i,j) that cross at least two different communities. For each of such edges, we consider the two largest communities C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} such that i∉C2i\notin C_{2} and j∉C1j\notin C_{1}, i∈C1i\in C_{1}, j∈C2j\in C_{2}, and extract the subgraph determined by C1∪C2C_{1}\cup C_{2}, which is connected since all the communities are connected. Finally, we divide the train and test sets by enforcing test examples to contain disjoint communities from those in the training set. In this experiment, due to computational limitations, we restrict our attention to the three smallest graphs in the SNAP collection (Youtube, DBLP and Amazon), and we restrict the largest community size to 800800 nodes, which is a conservative bound, since the average community size on these graphs is below 3030. We compare GNN’s performance with the Community-Affiliation Graph Model (AGM). The AGM is a generative model defined in [34] that allows overlapping communities where overlapping area have higher density. This was a statistical property observed in many real datasets with ground truth communities, but not present in generative models before AGM and was shown to outperform algorithms before that. Table 3 compares the performance, measured with a 3-class {1,2,1+2}\{1,2,1+2\} classification accuracy up to global permutation 1↔21\leftrightarrow 2. It illustrates the benefits of data-driven models that strike the right balance between expressive power to adapt to model misspecifications and structural assumptions of the task at hand.

7 Conclusion

In this work we have studied data-driven approaches to community detection with graph neural networks. Our results confirm that, even when the signal-to-noise ratio is at the lowest detectable regime, it is possible to backpropagate detection errors through a graph neural network that can ‘learn’ to extract the spectrum of appropriate operators. This is made possible by considering a family of graph operators that work effectively in sparsely connected graphs, in particular by considering a hierarchical extension that uses the non-backtracking operator in the line graph. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the optimization landscapes in the linearized regime, which shows an interesting transition from rugged to simple as the size of the graphs increase.

One word of caution is that our empirical results are inherently non-asymptotic, and further work is needed in order to confirm that learning is still possible as |V||V| grows. Nevertheless, our results open up interesting questions, namely understanding how our results on the energy landscape depend upon specific signal-to-noise ratios, or whether the network parameters can be interpreted mathematically. This could be useful in the study of computational-to-statistical gaps, where our model could be used to inquire about the form of computationally tractable approximations. Other directions of future research include the extension to the case where the number of communities is unknown and variable, and potentially increasing with nn, as well as applications to ranking and edge-cut problems.

Appendix A Background

A.1 Graph Min-Cuts and Spectral Clustering

We consider graphs G=(V,E)G=(V,E), modeling a system of N=|V|N=|V| elements presumed to exhibit some form of community structure. The adjacency matrix AA associated with GG is the N×NN\times N binary matrix such that Ai,j=1A_{i,j}=1 whenever (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E. We assume for simplicity undirected graphs, yielding symmetric adjacency matrices. The community structure is encoded in a discrete label vector s:V→{1,K}s:V\to\{1,K\} that assigns a community label to each node, and the goal is to estimate ss from observing the adjacency matrix.

In the setting of binary, associative communities, where s⁡(i)=±1s(i)=\pm 1, two nodes i,ji,j with s⁡(i)=s⁡(j)s(i)=s(j) are more likely to be connected (Ai,j=1A_{i,j}=1) than two nodes i,ji,j with s⁡(i)≠s⁡(j)s(i)\neq s(j). Thus a quantity of the form

∑i,j(1−s⁡(i)​s​(j))​Ai,j\sum_{i,j}(1-s(i)s(j))A_{i,j}

measures the cost associated with cutting the graph between communities encoded by ss that we wish to minimize under appropriate constraints [23]. Note that ∑i,jAi,j=sT​D​s\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}=s^{T}Ds, with D=diag​(A​𝟏)D=\text{diag}(A{\bf 1}) (called the degree matrix), so the cut cost can be expressed as a positive semidefinite quadratic form

mins⁡(i)=±1⁡sT​(D−A)​s=sT​Δ​s\min_{s(i)=\pm 1}s^{T}(D-A)s=s^{T}\Delta s

that we wish to minimize. This shows a fundamental connection between the community structure and the spectrum of certain linear operators of the graph, which provides a powerful and stable relaxation of the discrete combinatorial optimization problem of estimating the community labels for each node. In the case of the graph Laplacian Δ=D−A\Delta=D-A, its eigenvector associated with the smallest eigenvalue is trivial, but its Fiedler vector (the eigenvector associated with the second smallest eigenvalue) reveals important community information of the graph [23] under appropriate conditions, and is associated with the graph conductance [30] under certain normalization schemes.

For a given linear operator ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) extracted from the graph (that we assume symmetric), we are thus interested in extracting eigenvectors at the edge of its spectrum. A particularly simple algorithmic framework is given by the power iteration method. Indeed, the Fiedler vector of ℒ⁡(A)\mathcal{L}(A) can be obtained by first extracting the leading eigenvector vv of A~=‖ℒ⁡(A)‖−ℒ⁡(A)\tilde{A}=\|\mathcal{L}(A)\|-\mathcal{L}(A), and then iterating

y(n)=A~​w(n−1),w(n)=y(n)−⟨y(n),v⟩​v‖y(n)−⟨y(n),v⟩​v‖.y^{(n)}=\tilde{A}w^{(n-1)}~~,~w^{(n)}=\frac{y^{(n)}-\langle y^{(n)},v\rangle v}{\|y^{(n)}-\langle y^{(n)},v\rangle v\|}~.

Unrolling power iterations and recasting the resulting model as a trainable neural network is akin to the LISTA [11] sparse coding model, which unrolled iterative proximal splitting algorithms.

Despite the appeal of graph Laplacian spectral approaches, it is well known [17] that these methods fail in sparsely connected graphs. Indeed, in such scenarios, the eigenvectors of graph Laplacians concentrate on nodes with dominant degree, losing their ability to correlate with community structure. In order to overcome this important limitation, authors have resorted to ideas inspired from statistical physics, as explained next.

A.2 Probabilistic Graphical Models and Belief-Propagation

Graphs with labels on nodes and edges can be cast as a graphical model where the aim of clustering is to optimize label agreement. This can be seen as a posterior inference task. If we simply assume the graphical model is a Markov Random Field (MRF) with trivial compatibility functions for cliques greater than 2, the probability of a label configuration σ\sigma is given by

ℙ⁡(σ)=1𝒵​∏i∈Vϕi​(σi)​∏i​j∈Eψi​j​(σi,σj).\mathbb{P}(\sigma)=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\displaystyle\prod_{i\in V}\phi_{i}(\sigma_{i})\displaystyle\prod_{ij\in E}\psi_{ij}(\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j}). (6)

Generally, computing marginals of multivariate discrete distributions is exponentially hard. For instance, in the case of ℙ⁡(σi)\mathbb{P}(\sigma_{i}) we are summing over |X|n−1|X|^{n-1} terms (where XX is the state space of discrete variables). But if the graph is a tree, we can factorize the MRF more efficiently to compute the marginals in linear time via a dynamic programming method called the sum-product algorithm, also known as belief propagation (BP). An iteration of BP is given by

bi→j​(σi)=1Zi→j​ϕi​(σi)​∏k∈δ​i​\​j∑σk∈Xψi​k​(σi,σk)​bk→i​(σk).b_{i\rightarrow j}(\sigma_{i})=\frac{1}{Z_{i\rightarrow j}}\phi_{i}(\sigma_{i})\displaystyle\prod_{k\in\delta i\textbackslash j}\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma_{k}\in X}\psi_{ik}(\sigma_{i},\sigma_{k})b_{k\rightarrow i}(\sigma_{k}). (7)

The beliefs (bi→j​(σi)b_{i\rightarrow j}(\sigma_{i})) are interpreted as the marginal distributions of σi\sigma_{i}. Fixed points of BP can be used to recover marginals of the MRF above. In the case of the tree, the correspondence is exact: ℙi​(σi)=bi​(σi)\mathbb{P}_{i}(\sigma_{i})=b_{i}(\sigma_{i}). Some sparse graphs, like the Stochastic Blockmodel with constant degree[22] are locally similar to trees for such an approximation to be successful. BP approximates the MLE solutions but convergence is not guaranteed in graphs that are not trees. Furthermore, in order to apply BP, we need a generative model and the correct parameters of the model. If unknown, the parameters can be derived using expectation maximization, further adding complexity and instability to the method since iterations may learn parameters for which BP does not converge.

A.3 Non-backtracking operator and Bethe Hessian

The BP equations have a trivial fixed-point where every node takes equal probability in each group. Linearizing the BP equation around this point is equivalent to spectral clustering using the non-backtracking matrix (NB), a matrix defined on the edges of the graph that indicates whether two edges are adjacent and do not coincide. Spectral clustering using NB gives significant improvements over spectral clustering with versions of the Laplacians (L) and the adjacency matrix (A); High degree fluctuations drown out the signal of the informative eigenvalues in the case of A and L, whereas NB’s eigenvalues are confined to a disk in the complex plane, so its eigenvalues corresponding to community structure lay outside the disk and are easily distinguishable.

NB matrices are still not optimal in that they are matrices on the edge set, and are not symmetric (so cannot enjoy tools of numerical linear algebra for symmetric matrices). Recently Saade et al.[26] showed that a spectral method can do as well as BP in this regime, using the Bethe Hessian operator given by B​H​(r):=(r2−1)​𝕀−r​A+DBH(r):=(r^{2}-1)\mathbb{I}-rA+D (where rr is a scalar value). This is due to a one-to-one correspondence between the fixed points of BP and the stationary points of the Bethe free energy (corresponding Gibbs energy of the Bethe approximation)[37]. The Bethe Hessian is a scaling of the Hessian of the Bethe free energy at an extrema corresponding to the trivial fixed point of BP. Negative eigenvalues of B​H​(r)BH(r) correspond to phase transitions in the Ising model where new clusters become identifiable. This all gives theoretical motivation for why [𝕀,D,A][\mathbb{I},D,A] defined in Section 3 are a good family of generators to do spectral clustering on. In the case of the SBM, they generate the Bethe Hessian which can achieve community detection down to the information theoretic threshold. The GNN is capable of expressing spectral approximations of complicated functions of [𝕀,D,A][\mathbb{I},D,A], and performing nonlinear power method iterations in order to infer global structure (for instance community structure). Furthermore, unlike belief propagation, the method does not require a generative model, oftentimes requires a lot statistical analysis to motivate and is exposed to model misspecifications when deployed on real data. Instead, our framework finds structure in a data driven way, learning it from the available training data.

A.4 Stochastic Block Model

We briefly review the main properties needed in our analysis, and refer the interested reader to [1] for an excellent recent review. The Stochastic Blockmodel (SBM) is a random graph model denoted by S​B​M​(n,p,q,K)SBM(n,p,q,K). Implicitly there is an F:V→{1,…,K}F:V\rightarrow\{1,...,K\} associated with each SBM graph, which assigns community labels to each vertex. One obtains a graph from this generative model by starting with nn vertices and connecting any two vertices u,vu,v independently at random with probability pp if F⁡(v)=F⁡(u)F(v)=F(u), and with probability qq if F⁡(v)≠F⁡(u)F(v)\neq F(u). We say the SBM is balanced if the communities are the same size. Let Fn¯:V→{1,…,K}\bar{F_{n}}:V\rightarrow\{1,...,K\} be our predicted community labels for SBM(n,p,q.K)SBM(n,p,q.K), FnF_{n}’s give exact recovery on a sequence {S​B​M​(n,p,q)}n\{SBM(n,p,q)\}_{n} if ℙ(Fn=Fn¯)→n1\mathbb{P}(F_{n}=\bar{F_{n}})\rightarrow_{n}1, and give detection ∃ϵ>0:ℙ(|Fn−Fn¯|≥1/k+ϵ)→n1\exists\epsilon>0:\mathbb{P}(|F_{n}-\bar{F_{n}}|\geq 1/k+\epsilon)\rightarrow_{n}1 (i.e Fn¯\bar{F_{n}}’s do better than random guessing).

It is harder to tell communities apart if pp is close to qq (if p=qp=q we just get an Erdős Renyi random graph, which has no communities). In the two community case, It was shown that exact recovery is possible on S​B​M​(n,p=a​log⁡nn,q=b​log⁡nn)SBM(n,p=\frac{a\log n}{n},q=\frac{b\log n}{n}) if and only if a+b2≥1+a​b\frac{a+b}{2}\geq 1+\sqrt{ab} [21, 2]. For exact recovery to be possible, p,qp,q must grow at least O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) or else the sequence of graphs will not to be connected, and thus vertex labels will be underdetermined. There is no information-computation gap in this regime, so there are polynomial time algorithms when recovery is possible ([1][21]). In the much sparser regime of constant degree SBM (n,p=an,q=bnn,p=\frac{a}{n},q=\frac{b}{n}), detection is the best we hope for. The constant degree regime is also of most interest to us for real world applications, as most large datasets have bounded degree and are extremely sparse. It is also a very challenging regime; spectral approaches using the Laplacian in its various (un)normalized forms and the adjacency matrix, as well as SDP methods cannot detect communities in this regime[1] due to large fluctuations in the degree distribution that prevent eigenvectors form concentrating on the clusters. [6] first proposed the BP algorithm on the SBM, which was proven to yield Bayesian optimal values in [5]

In the constant degree regime with balanced kk communities, the Kesten-Stigum threshold is given by S​N​R:=(a−b)2/(k⁡(a+(k+1)​b))SNR:=(a-b)^{2}/(k(a+(k+1)b)) [1]. It has been shown for k=2k=2 that S​N​R=1SNR=1 is both the information theoretic and efficient computational threshold where belief propagation (BP) via a polynomial time algorithm. For k>4k>4 a gap emerges between the information theoretic threshold and computational one. It’s conjectured that no polynomial time algorithm exist for S​N​R<1SNR<1, while a BP algorithm works for S​N​R>1SNR>1[1, 6]. The existence of the gap was shown by [1] by proving a non-polynomial algorithm can do detection for some S​N​R<1SNR<1.

As a step towards proving Theorem 5.1, we first prove the following main lemma, Lemma B.1, which claims that under the same conditions as in 5.1, any local maximum of LnL_{n} is close to the global maximum of L~n\tilde{L}_{n}, where the closeness is measured by the cosine distance.

Subsection B.1 is devoted to proving this lemma, and subsection B.2 is devoted to proving Theorem 5.1 as a consequence of this lemma.

∀γ∈ℝM\forall\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{M},

limn→∞‖∇2Sn​(γ)−∇2S~n​(γ)‖=0\begin{split}\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}S_{n}(\gamma)-\nabla^{2}\tilde{S}_{n}(\gamma)\|=0\end{split} (24)

where

(γT​γ)3​Bn​γ​γT​BnT−(γT​Bn​γ)3​γ​γT=(γT​γ)3​(Bn−I)​γ​γT​Bn+(γT​γ)3​γ​γT​(Bn−I)+[(γT​γ)3−(γT​Bn​γ)3]​γ​γT=(γT​γ)3​Δ​Bn​γ​γT​Bn+(γT​γ)3​γ​γT​Δ​Bn+[(γTBnγ)2(−γTΔBnγ)γγT+(γTBnγ)(−γTΔBnγ)γγT+(−γTΔBnγ)γγT]\begin{split}(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}B_{n}\gamma\gamma^{T}B_{n}^{T}-(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{3}\gamma\gamma^{T}=&(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}(B_{n}-I)\gamma\gamma^{T}B_{n}+(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}\gamma\gamma^{T}(B_{n}-I)\\ &+[(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}-(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{3}]\gamma\gamma^{T}\\ =&(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}\Delta B_{n}\gamma\gamma^{T}B_{n}+(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}\gamma\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\\ &+[(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{2}(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}+(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}\\ &+(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}]\end{split} (35)

Hence,

H3=(γTAnγ)[(γT​γ)3​Δ​Bn​γ​γT​Bn+(γT​γ)3​γ​γT​Δ​Bn+(−γT​Δ​Bn​γ)​γ​γT(γT​Bn​γ)3​(γT​γ)3+(−γT​Δ​Bn​γ)​γ​γT(γT​Bn​γ)2​(γT​γ)+(−γT​Δ​Bn​γ)​γ​γT(γT​Bn​γ)​(γT​γ)2]\begin{split}H_{3}=&(\gamma^{T}A_{n}\gamma)[\frac{(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}\Delta B_{n}\gamma\gamma^{T}B_{n}+(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}\gamma\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}+(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}}{(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{3}(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{3}}\\ &+\frac{(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}}{(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{2}(\gamma^{T}\gamma)}+\frac{(-\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)\gamma\gamma^{T}}{(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{2}}]\end{split} (36)

Thus,

‖H3‖≤|λ1​(An)|‖γ‖2​[1|λM3​(Bn)|​(‖Δ​Bn‖​|λ1​(Bn)|+2​‖Δ​Bn‖)+1λM2​(Bn)​‖Δ​Bn‖+1|λM​(Bn)|​‖Δ​Bn‖]\|H_{3}\|\leq\frac{|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|}{\|\gamma\|^{2}}[\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}^{3}(B_{n})|}(\|\Delta B_{n}\||\lambda_{1}(B_{n})|+2\|\Delta B_{n}\|)+\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}^{2}(B_{n})}\|\Delta B_{n}\|+\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|}\|\Delta B_{n}\|] (37)

For the last term,

H4=[−2​(γT​γ)​(γT​Δ​Bn​γ)​I−(γT​Δ​Bn​γ)2​I]​An​γ​γT​Bn+(γT​Bn​γ)2​An​γ​γT​Δ​Bn(γT​Bn​γ)2​(γT​γ)2H_{4}=\frac{[-2(\gamma^{T}\gamma)(\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)I-(\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)^{2}I]A_{n}\gamma\gamma^{T}B_{n}+(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{2}A_{n}\gamma\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}}{(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)^{2}(\gamma^{T}\gamma)^{2}} (39)

Applying generalized Hölder’s inequality, we obtain

𝔼​‖H4‖≤1‖γ‖2[2(𝔼1|λM​(Bn)|6)13(𝔼|λ1(An)|3)13(𝔼∥ΔBn∥6)16(𝔼|λ1(Bn)|6)16+(𝔼​1|λM​(Bn)|6)13​(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|6)16​(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖6)13​(𝔼​|λ1​(Bn)|6)16+(𝔼1|λM​(Bn)|6)13(𝔼|λ1(An)|6)16(𝔼∥ΔBn∥6)16(𝔼|λ1(Bn)|6)13]\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\|H_{4}\|\leq\frac{1}{\|\gamma\|^{2}}&[2(\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{6}})^{\frac{1}{3}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(B_{n})|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}\\ &+(\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{6}})^{\frac{1}{3}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{6})^{\frac{1}{3}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(B_{n})|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}\\ &+(\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{6}})^{\frac{1}{3}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{6})^{\frac{1}{6}}(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(B_{n})|^{6})^{\frac{1}{3}}]\end{split} (41)

The rest of this proof is similar to the argument in the proof of the previous lemma: By the assumptions of the theorem, ∃M1,M2\exists M_{1},M_{2} such that 𝔼[|λ1(An)|6]≤M1,𝔼[1|λM​(Bn)|6]≤M2,∀n\mathbb{E}[|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{6}]\leq M_{1},\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{6}}]\leq M_{2},\forall n. Thus, 𝔼[|λ1(An)|3]≤M1,𝔼[1|λM​(Bn)|3]≤M2,∀n\mathbb{E}[|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3}]\leq\sqrt{M_{1}},\mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|^{3}}]\leq\sqrt{M_{2}},\forall n. Since it is also assumed that limn→∞𝔼⁡[‖Δ​Bn‖6]=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{6}]=0, there also is limn→∞𝔼⁡[‖Δ​Bn‖3]=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3}]=0. Moreover, as Bn=I+Δ​BnB_{n}=I+\Delta B_{n}, we know that 𝔼⁡[|λ1​(Bn)|6]\mathbb{E}[|\lambda_{1}(B_{n})|^{6}] is uniformly bounded as well.

Therefore, we have limn→∞‖∇2Sn​(γ)−∇2S~n​(γ)‖=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\nabla^{2}S_{n}(\gamma)-\nabla^{2}\tilde{S}_{n}(\gamma)\|=0. ∎

B.2 Proof of Theorem 5.1 as a consequence of Lemma B.1

Let βg\beta_{g} denote the global maximum (or one of the global maxima) of LnL_{n}. Let γl=TnT​βl,γg=TnT​βg\gamma_{l}=T_{n}^{T}\beta_{l},\gamma_{g}=T_{n}^{T}\beta_{g} and γ~g=TnT​β~g\tilde{\gamma}_{g}=T_{n}^{T}\tilde{\beta}_{g}.

Note that

|Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤|Ln​(βl)−L~n​(βl)|+|L~n​(βl)−L~n​(βg)|+|L~n​(βg)−Ln​(βg)||L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})| (42)

If L~n​(βl)≥L~n​(βg)\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})\geq\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g}), then L~n​(βl)−L~n​(β~g)≥L~n​(βl)−L~n​(βg)≥0\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})\geq\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})\geq 0, and so |Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤|Ln​(βl)−L~n​(βl)|+|L~n​(βl)−L~n​(β~g)|+|L~n​(βg)−Ln​(βg)||L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|. Otherwise, there is L~n​(βl)<L~n​(βg)\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})<\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g}), while Ln​(βl)≥Ln​(βg)L_{n}(\beta_{l})\geq L_{n}(\beta_{g}). Then |Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤|Ln​(βl)−L~n​(βl)|+|L~n​(βg)−Ln​(βg)|≤|Ln​(βl)−L~n​(βl)|+|L~n​(βl)−L~n​(β~g)|+|L~n​(βg)−Ln​(βg)||L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|.

Hence, in both cases, there is

|Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤|Ln​(βl)−L~n​(βl)|+|L~n​(βl)−L~n​(β~g)|+|L~n​(βg)−Ln​(βg)||L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})|+|\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})| (43)

Now, we try to bound the three terms on the right hand side separately. Lemma B.7 allows us to bound the first and the third term:

Lemma B.7.

∀β\forall\beta,

|Ln​(β)−L~n​(β)|≤(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖3)13⋅(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|3)13⋅(𝔼​|1λM​(Bn)|3)13|L_{n}(\beta)-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta)|\leq(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}(B_{n})}|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}} (44)
Proof of Lemma B.7.

Let γ=TnT​β\gamma=T_{n}^{T}\beta.

|Ln​(β)−L~n​(β)|=Sn​(γ)−S~n​(γ)=|𝔼​(γT​Δ​Bn​γ)​(γT​An​γ)(γT​Bn​γ)​(γT​γ)|≤𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖​|λ1​(An)||λM​(Bn)|\begin{split}|L_{n}(\beta)-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta)|=&S_{n}(\gamma)-\tilde{S}_{n}(\gamma)\\ =&|\mathbb{E}\frac{(\gamma^{T}\Delta B_{n}\gamma)(\gamma^{T}A_{n}\gamma)}{(\gamma^{T}B_{n}\gamma)(\gamma^{T}\gamma)}|\\ \leq&\mathbb{E}\frac{\|\Delta B_{n}\||\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|}{|\lambda_{M}(B_{n})|}\end{split} (45)

Thus, we get the desired lemma by the generalized Hölder’s inequality.

∎

Following the notations in the proof of Lemma B.3, we write γl=∑i=1dαi​γ^i\gamma_{l}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\alpha_{i}\hat{\gamma}_{i}. Note that γ~g=γ^1\tilde{\gamma}_{g}=\hat{\gamma}_{1}, and cos⁡(γ,γ^i)=α¯i\cos(\gamma,\hat{\gamma}_{i})=\bar{\alpha}_{i}. Thus,

L~n​(βl)=S~n​(γl)=∑i=1dαi2​li∑i=1dαi2=∑i=1dα¯i2​li\begin{split}\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})=&\tilde{S}_{n}(\gamma_{l})\\ =&\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\alpha_{i}^{2}l_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{d}\alpha_{i}^{2}}\\ =&\sum_{i=1}^{d}\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{2}l_{i}\end{split} (46)

Since YnY_{n} is positive semidefinite, 𝔼​Yn\mathbb{E}Y_{n} is also positive semidifinite, and hence A¯n=TnT​𝔼​Yn​(Tn−1)T\bar{A}_{n}=T_{n}^{T}\mathbb{E}Y_{n}(T_{n}^{-1})^{T} is positive semidefinite as well. This means that li≥0,∀i∈{1,…,M}l_{i}\geq 0,\forall i\in\{1,...,M\}. Since L~n​(βg~)=S~n​(γ~g)=S~n​(γ^1)=l1\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta_{g}})=\tilde{S}_{n}(\tilde{\gamma}_{g})=\tilde{S}_{n}(\hat{\gamma}_{1})=l_{1}, there is

|L~n​(βg~)−L~n​(βl)|≤(1−α¯12)​l1|\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta_{g}})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{l})|\leq(1-\bar{\alpha}_{1}^{2})l_{1} (47)

Therefore,

|Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|≤2​(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖3)13⋅(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|3)13⋅(𝔼​|1λM​(Bn)|3)13+(1−cos2⁡(γl,γ~g))​λ1​(A¯n)|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\leq 2(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}(B_{n})}|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}+(1-\cos^{2}(\gamma_{l},\tilde{\gamma}_{g}))\lambda_{1}(\bar{A}_{n}) (48)

On the other hand,

|Ln​(βg)−L~n​(β~g)|≤max⁡{|Ln​(βg)−L~n​(βg)|,|Ln​(β~g)−L~n​(β~g)|}≤(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖3)13⋅(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|3)13⋅(𝔼​|1λM​(Bn)|3)13\begin{split}|L_{n}(\beta_{g})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})|\leq\max\{|L_{n}(\beta_{g})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\beta_{g})|,|L_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})-\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})|\}\\ \leq(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}(B_{n})}|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\end{split} (49)

Hence,

Ln​(βg)≥L~n​(β~g)−(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖3)13⋅(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|3)13⋅(𝔼​|1λM​(Bn)|3)13≥λ1​(A¯n)−(𝔼​‖Δ​Bn‖3)13⋅(𝔼​|λ1​(An)|3)13⋅(𝔼​|1λM​(Bn)|3)13\begin{split}L_{n}(\beta_{g})\geq\tilde{L}_{n}(\tilde{\beta}_{g})-(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}(B_{n})}|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\\ \geq\lambda_{1}(\bar{A}_{n})-(\mathbb{E}\|\Delta B_{n}\|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\lambda_{1}(A_{n})|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot(\mathbb{E}|\frac{1}{\lambda_{M}(B_{n})}|^{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}\end{split} (50)

By Lemma B.1, cos2⁡(γl,γ~g)→1\cos^{2}(\gamma_{l},\tilde{\gamma}_{g})\to 1 as n→∞n\to\infty. As a consequence of this lemma as well as the assumptions in the theorem, |Ln​(βl)−Ln​(βg)|→0|L_{n}(\beta_{l})-L_{n}(\beta_{g})|\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty while Ln​(βg)→λ1​(A¯n)>0L_{n}(\beta_{g})\to\lambda_{1}(\bar{A}_{n})>0 as n→∞n\to\infty. We have thus proved the theorem.

Appendix C Further Experiments on the SBM

We report here our experiments on the SBM mixture, generated with

G∼S​B​M​(n=1000,p=k​d¯−q,q∼Unif​(0,d¯−d¯),C=2),G\sim SBM(n=1000,p=k\bar{d}-q,q\sim\text{Unif}(0,\bar{d}-\sqrt{\bar{d}}),C=2)~,

where the average degree d¯\bar{d} is either fixed constant or also randomized with d¯∼Unif​(1,t)\bar{d}\sim\text{Unif}(1,t). Figure 2 shows the overlap obtained by our model compared with several baselines. Our GNN model is either competitive with BH or beats BH, which achieves the state of the art along with BP [26], despite not having any access to the underlying generative model (especially in cases where GNN was trained on a mixture of SBM and thus must be able to generalize the rr parameter in BH). They all beat by a wide margin spectral clustering methods using the symmetric Laplacian (Ls) and power method (pm) applied to ‖B​H‖​𝕀−B​H\|BH\|\mathbb{I}-BH using the same number of layers as our model. Thus GNN’s ability to predict labels goes beyond approximating spectral decomposition via learning the optimal rr for B​H​(r)BH(r). The model architecture allows it to learn a higher dimensional function of the optimal perturbation of the multiscale adjacency basis, as well as nonlinear power iterations, that amplify the informative signals in the spectrum; In a data driven way it can generalize the problem without needing to study a generative model.
